81275417.title: 2025 Enderlin tornado
81275417.extract:
On the night of June 20, 2025, a large and extremely violent EF5 tornado moved through rural North Dakota, United States, passing near the community of Enderlin. Part of a larger outbreak and derecho sequence that occurred across the northern Great Plains between June 19 and 22, the tornado, referred to as Enderlin Tornado #1 by the National Weather Service (NWS), was the first to be rated EF5 on the Enhanced Fujita scale since the tornado that struck Moore, Oklahoma, on May 20, 2013, ending a 12-year-long period without tornadoes rated EF5. It killed three people, becoming the deadliest tornado to occur in North Dakota since the F4 tornado that struck Elgin in 1978. 
The tornado was given a preliminary rating of EF3, with the highest wind speeds estimated at 160 mph (260 km/h). However, this rating was upgraded to EF5 following additional surveys and forensic damage analysis for the tipping and lofting of several fully-loaded grain hopper cars and empty tanker cars conducted in association with wind damage experts and researchers at the Northern Tornadoes Project. The tornado also destroyed multiple farmhouses and obliterated a forest along the Maple River. A statewide disaster was declared by the Governor of North Dakota following the tornado outbreak. In September, federal disaster relief was approved, but was stalled amid the 2025 United States federal government shutdown. Locals and other organizations volunteered to help with the recovery efforts.


== Meteorological synopsis ==
On June 15, the Storm Prediction Center (SPC) on its Day 6 outlook forecasted that a shortwave, mid-level ridge would move into the upper Mississippi River Valley and remain over the region throughout June 20. Beneath the ridge, a moist and unstable airmass was expected to be in place from the lower to mid-Missouri River Valley, northeastward into the western Great Lakes region. Instability and deep-layer wind shear were sufficient for a localized severe weather threat, though uncertainties remained on where the greatest potential for convection was.
A seasonally strong mid-level trough was forecast to eject over the Northern Plains on June 20, which featured moderate upper-level divergence to promote lift and deep-layer shear. The Storm Prediction Center (SPC) Day 2 outlook mentioned that "a small area of uncapped and very unstable air mass, perhaps over northeast SD and southeast ND. Here, a conditional supercell and tornado risk will exist ... very large hail and tornadoes appear likely." 
At 8:15 p.m. on June 20, the SPC noted that storms developing over eastern North Dakota, while potentially elevated, were entering a favorable environment to become surface-based and pose a greater risk for hazards of severe weather. These storms followed to the southwest of a lone supercell already producing large hail. As these storms moved towards the Red River, favorable low-level wind conditions were forecast to support an increased threat of tornadoes, albeit in a smaller and localized region. At this time, forecasters noted that tornadoes could be strong, with the most likely peak wind speeds from any tornado being 120–150 mph (190–240 km/h). A few tornadoes touched down before the Enderlin tornado, including an EF3 tornado near Spiritwood and two EF2 tornadoes near Valley City and Fort Ransom, respectively; both moved in a southeasterly direction towards the Enderlin area. The SPC released a mesoscale discussion concerning this with the potential for EF2/EF3–strength tornadoes to occur as a result.


== Tornado summary ==


=== Formation and peak intensity ===

The tornado initially touched down at 11:02 p.m. Central Daylight Time (UTC–5) along 58th Street SE, 3.8 miles (6.1 km) south of Enderlin in Ransom County. After snapping tree branches at EF0 intensity at its touchdown point, the tornado intensified and widened as it moved east-northeastward across County Road 55 through open fields. The tornado then impacted the ADM Edible Bean Specialties grain elevator facility at the corner of 136th Avenue SE and County Road 136 at EF2 strength, snapping large trees and destroying an outbuilding. The tornado then began a rapid intensification and widening phase as it turned northeastward. It reached EF5 intensity as it crossed CPKC's Elbow Lake Subdivision southeast of Enderlin, derailing numerous train cars on a stopped freight train. Five train cars were lofted, and 28 more were tipped over. A home that was on the edge of the path sustained minor EF0 damage to its roof as well.
The tornado then turned north-northeastward, growing to its peak width of 1.05 miles (1.69 km). It blew over a cell tower that was anchored by four cables into the ground, completely scoured crop fields, and snapped large trees, debarking some of them. It also leveled an unoccupied farmhouse, shifted another house off its foundation, and damaged or destroyed outbuildings. Damage in this area was rated EF2 to EF3. The tornado then inflicted violent EF4 damage to trees as it moved along the Maple River and approached ND 46. An entire forest of trees along the river was leveled, with only stubs of the trees left behind. Severe debarking of trees was also noted, with some of them being "sandpapered," and some trees were lofted with the root ball attached, including one whose original location could not be determined.

The violent tornado then crossed ND 46 into Cass County, and devastated two homes, with two deaths occurring in this area. The first home, along with a well-built detached garage nearby, was obliterated and swept away with all the debris scattered downwind of both structures. It was acknowledged that the tornado may have been even stronger at this location, but insufficient anchoring prevented a rating higher than mid-range EF4. The second house, located approximately 300 yd (270 m) to the west of the first along 140th Avenue SE, along with nearby outbuildings, was leveled. The tornado then crossed over the Maple River, leveling another swath of trees.


=== Dissipation ===
The tornado then turned due north and paralleled 140th Avenue SE, snapping trees and damaging crops at EF2 strength. It also caused EF1 damage as it crossed along 52nd Street SE, shattering the windows of a home and inflicting roof damage to a mobile home. The tornado then turned north-northwestward, leveling another farmhouse at high-end EF3 strength, and snapping numerous trees; one person was killed in the house. After snapping more trees at EF2 strength, the tornado turned northwestward and toppled four tall steel electrical transmission towers at low-end EF3 strength; it also snapped wooden power poles in this area as it crossed County Road 38. The tornado then quickly narrowed and weakened as it sharply looped back to the south along the southern end of the Utke Waterfowl Production Area, crossing County Road 16 twice, and snapping some additional hardwood tree trunks at EF2 strength before dissipating just west of the 50th Street SE and 138th Avenue SE intersection at 11:21 p.m. Central Daylight Time (UTC–5), approximately 5 miles (8.0 km) southwest of Alice.

Overall, the tornado was on the ground for 19 minutes, had a path length of 12.10 miles (19.47 km), and reached a peak width of 1.05 miles (1.69 km). According to the Enderlin–Sheldon Fire Department, 10 homes sustained some form of damage from the storm. Shortly after the dissipation of the Enderlin tornado, a second large tornado formed just east of the first tornado's path at 11:22 p.m. CDT. Moving southeast, this second tornado caused EF2 damage to trees and outbuildings across a 6.82 miles (10.98 km) path before dissipating at 11:34 p.m. CDT. 


== Aftermath ==


=== Casualties and recovery efforts ===

Governor of North Dakota Kelly Armstrong declared a statewide disaster following the tornado, activating the state's "Emergency Operations Plan". On June 24, over 150 volunteers joined in a joint cleanup operation. The International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement sent disaster teams to Enderlin to aid in recovery efforts, and volunteers from the Northern Plains UAS Test Site deployed an Unmanned Aerial System to help residents find personal items that had been lost as a result of the tornado. North Bank set up a fund for victims of the tornado, and the Enderlin Fire Department assisted in initial clean-up efforts. 
The town of Enderlin itself was not struck by the tornado, although it lost power due to the storm. Debris fallout from the tornado extended to Moorhead, Minnesota, 40 miles (64 km) from where they originated. Here, a photograph and a tax return form, both belonging to two different people killed in the tornado, were found after the storm carried them there.
The 2025 United States federal government shutdown, which was ongoing at the time of the tornado's upgrade to an EF5 rating, made disaster assistance unavailable until the shutdown ended; President Donald Trump had approved Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) disaster relief to assist the month prior.
The tornado killed three people, all in the vicinity of Enderlin. The three deaths occurred at two different locations along the tornado's path. It was the deadliest tornado to strike the state since 1978, when an F4 tornado killed five people in Elgin.


=== Rating upgrade ===
The National Weather Service office in Grand Forks, North Dakota, originally gave the tornado an EF3 rating. Peak winds were estimated to be around 160 miles per hour (260 km/h).
On October 6, 2025, the NWS Grand Forks, with assistance from several engineers including Timothy P. Marshall, released a revised survey of the Enderlin tornado. Its final rating was upgraded to EF5 on the Enhanced Fujita scale, with maximum winds estimated to be over 210 miles per hour (340 km/h; 94 m/s). The tornado also caused high-end damage in other areas, although the construction at these areas limited said damage points to being upgraded from high-end EF3 to mid-range EF4. The strong winds correlated to the indicated winds on the WSR-88D Storm-Relative Velocity data from the Grand Forks radar site.
The intensity of the tornado was calculated from the distances the train cars were lofted and thrown. This new method was outlined in a study authored by a team of scientists and engineers of the Northern Tornadoes Project, and published in the peer-reviewed journal Monthly Weather Review in 2024. In this study, researchers with the Northern Tornadoes Project found an empirical relationship between the distance large and compact objects, such as farm equipment and vehicles, were thrown by the tornado, and damage indicators corresponding to ratings on the Enhanced Fujita scale. The study used tornadoes throughout Canada as examples, and found that these tornadoes, which occurred near Alonsa, Manitoba on August 3, 2018, Scarth, Manitoba, on August 7, 2020, and Didsbury, Alberta, on July 1, 2023, were all most likely of EF5 intensity, based on Monte Carlo simulations on cumulative distribution functions showing the likelihood of lofting at each wind speed based on the weight and distance of objects lofted. 
In all, it was determined that 33 cars on the train derailed; 19 of them were fully loaded grain hopper cars weighing up to 286,000 lb (130,000 kg) that were all tipped over, with one of them being pulled off the tracks and thrown into an adjacent field. The other 14 cars were empty tanker cars weighing up to 72,000 lb (33,000 kg). Four of the cars were thrown out into the field, including one that was tossed 600–1,000 ft (180–300 m), landing 475.7 ft (145.0 m) away from the previous tank car it was attached to. Wheel sets from the derailed cars detached at the locations where the cars came off the rails. Collaborating with wind damage experts and the Northern Tornadoes Project, the NWS determined that winds of 230 mph (370 km/h) were needed to tip over a fully loaded grain car and winds of over 266 mph (428 km/h) to throw a tank car 475.7 ft (145.0 m).  In addition, extreme radar measurements were observed around the time that EF5-rated damage was being inflicted. It was also determined that the train cars were lofted twice as far as the EF5 threshold distance and four times heavier than the heaviest object model in the reanalysis. Prior to the reanalysis, the damage to the train cars had been left unrated since train cars are not standard damage indicators.

Melinda Beerends, meteorologist in charge of the National Weather Service office in Grand Forks, stated that "In the last kind of 12 years, there's been several strong tornadoes that have come close, but there haven't been known damage indicators at that time to support the EF5 rating ... it's hard sometimes to get tornadoes to hit something." The upgraded rating ended the EF5 drought that had begun following the May 2013 Moore, Oklahoma, tornado. The tornado was additionally the first F5 or EF5-rated tornado to occur in the month of June in the United States since the 1992 tornado near Chandler, Minnesota.

List of F5, EF5, and IF5 tornadoes

Fargo tornado – another F5 tornado that hit North Dakota exactly 68 years before

Here, a conditional supercell and tornado risk will exist {{Omission}} very large hail and tornadoes appear likely."{{Cite web |title=Storm Prediction Center Jun 19, 2025 1730 UTC Day 2 Convective Outlook |url=https://www.spc.noaa.gov/products/outlook/archive/2025/day2otlk_20250619_1730.html |access-date=June 22, 2025 |website=[[Storm Prediction Center]]}} At 8:15{{nbsp}}p.m. on June 20, the SPC noted that storms developing over eastern North Dakota, while potentially elevated, were entering a favorable environment to become surface-based and pose a greater risk for hazards of severe weather. These storms followed to the southwest of a lone [[supercell]] already producing large hail. As these storms moved towards the [[Red River of the North|Red River]], favorable low-level wind conditions were forecast to support an increased threat of tornadoes, albeit in a smaller and localized region. At this time, forecasters noted that tornadoes could be strong, with the most likely peak wind speeds from any tornado being {{cvt|120–150|mph|km/h}}.{{Cite web |last=Moore |first=Andrew |date=June 20, 2025 |title=Storm Prediction Center Mesoscale Discussion 1386 |url=https://www.spc.noaa.gov/products/md/md1386.html |access-date=October 8, 2025 |website=[[Storm Prediction Center]]}} A few tornadoes touched down before the Enderlin tornado, including an EF3 tornado near [[Spiritwood, North Dakota|Spiritwood]] and two EF2 tornadoes near [[Valley City, North Dakota|Valley City]] and [[Fort Ransom, North Dakota|Fort Ransom]], respectively; both moved in a southeasterly direction towards the [[Enderlin, North Dakota|Enderlin]] area.{{Cite web |last=Moore |first=Andrew |date=June 20, 2025 |title=Storm Prediction Center Mesoscale Discussion 1390 |url=https://www.spc.noaa.gov/products/md/md1390.html |access-date=October 8, 2025 |website=[[Storm Prediction Center]]}}{{Cite web |title=June 20, 2025 Summary; Updated: 7/18/2025 12:00pm |url=https://www.weather.gov/fgf/2025_06_20_Summary |access-date=October 8, 2025 |website=[[National Weather Service Grand Forks, North Dakota]] |language=EN-US}} The SPC released a mesoscale discussion concerning this with the potential for EF2/EF3–strength tornadoes to occur as a result. == Tornado summary == ===Formation and peak intensity=== [[File:Jun 21 0408z Enderlin EF5.png|left|thumb|A radar scan of the tornado and parent supercell near peak intensity. Note the [[hook echo]] (left) and extremely powerful [[tornado vortex signature]] (right).]] The tornado initially touched down at 11:02{{nbsp}}p.m. [[Central Daylight Time]] ([[UTC]]–5) along 58th Street SE, {{convert|3.8|mi|km}} south of [[Enderlin, North Dakota|Enderlin]] in [[Ransom County, North Dakota|Ransom County]]. After snapping tree branches at EF0 intensity at its touchdown point, the tornado intensified and widened as it moved east-northeastward across County Road 55 through open fields.{{cite report |url=https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=PNSFGF&e=202506232108 |title=NWS Damage Survey for 6/20/2025 Enderlin Tornadoes |author=[[National Weather Service]] in Grand Forks, North Dakota |date=June 23, 2025 |publisher=Iowa Environmental Mesonet |access-date=June 27, 2025}}{{cite web |title=Damage Assessment Toolkit (DAT) |url=https://apps.dat.noaa.gov/StormDamage/DamageViewer/ |access-date=October 6, 2025 |website=[[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]] |quote=Set Begin Date at June 20, 2025 and End Date at June 21, 2025}} The tornado then impacted the ADM Edible Bean Specialties grain elevator facility at the corner of 136th Avenue SE and County Road 136 at EF2 strength, snapping large trees and destroying an outbuilding. The tornado then began a rapid intensification and widening phase as it turned northeastward. It reached EF5 intensity as it crossed [[Canadian Pacific Kansas City|CPKC]]'s [[Elbow Lake Subdivision]] southeast of Enderlin, derailing numerous train cars on a stopped freight train. Five train cars were lofted, and 28 more were tipped over.{{Cite web |last=Rice |first=Doyle |date=October 6, 2025 |title=USA's record tornado 'drought' ends with 210 mph monster in Dakotas |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/weather/2025/10/06/america-ef5-tornado-drought-enderlin-north-dakota/86550272007/ |access-date=October 7, 2025 |website=[[USA Today]] |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |last=Sandoval |first=Tadeo Ruiz |date=October 8, 2025 |title=Enderlin tornado earns rare EF-5 category after derailing 33 train cars |url=https://www.mprnews.org/story/2025/10/08/enderlin-tornado-earns-rare-ef5-category-after-derailing-33-train-cars |access-date=October 9, 2025 |website=[[MPR News]] |language=en}} A home that was on the edge of the path sustained minor EF0 damage to its roof as well. The tornado then turned north-northeastward, growing to its peak width of {{Convert|1.05|miles|km|abbr=on}}. It blew over a cell tower that was anchored by four cables into the ground, completely scoured crop fields, and snapped large trees, debarking some of them. It also leveled an unoccupied farmhouse, shifted another house off its foundation, and damaged or destroyed outbuildings. Damage in this area was rated EF2 to EF3. The tornado then inflicted violent EF4 damage to trees as it moved along the [[Maple River (North Dakota)|Maple River]] and approached [[North Dakota Highway 46|ND 46]]. An entire forest of trees along the river was leveled, with only stubs of the trees left behind. Severe debarking of trees was also noted, with some of them being "sandpapered," and some trees were lofted with the root ball attached, including one whose original location could not be determined. [[File:Aerial image of a home swept away at EF4 intensity near Enderlin.jpg|thumb|244x244px|Home east of Enderlin swept away at mid-range EF4 intensity, two fatalities were recorded here.]] The violent tornado then crossed ND 46 into [[Cass County, North Dakota|Cass County]], and devastated two homes, with two deaths occurring in this area. The first home, along with a well-built detached garage nearby, was obliterated and swept away with all the debris scattered downwind of both structures. It was acknowledged that the tornado may have been even stronger at this location, but insufficient anchoring prevented a rating higher than mid-range EF4. The second house, located approximately {{Convert|300|yd|m|abbr=on}} to the west of the first along 140th Avenue SE, along with nearby outbuildings, was leveled.{{Cite web |title=At least 3 dead in North Dakota after severe weather swept across region |url=https://abcnews.go.com/US/3-dead-north-dakota-severe-weather-sweeps-region/story?id=123068015 |access-date=June 24, 2025 |website=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]] |language=en}} The tornado then crossed over the Maple River, leveling another swath of trees. ===Dissipation=== The tornado then turned due north and paralleled 140th Avenue SE, snapping trees and damaging crops at EF2 strength. It also caused EF1 damage as it crossed along 52nd Street SE, shattering the windows of a home and inflicting roof damage to a mobile home. The tornado then turned north-northwestward, leveling another farmhouse at high-end EF3 strength, and snapping numerous trees; one person was killed in the house. After snapping more trees at EF2 strength, the tornado turned northwestward and toppled four tall steel electrical transmission towers at low-end EF3 strength; it also snapped wooden power poles in this area as it crossed County Road 38. The tornado then quickly narrowed and weakened as it sharply looped back to the south along the southern end of the Utke Waterfowl Production Area, crossing County Road 16 twice, and snapping some additional hardwood tree trunks at EF2 strength before dissipating just west of the 50th Street SE and 138th Avenue SE intersection at 11:21{{nbsp}}p.m. [[Central Daylight Time]] ([[UTC]]–5), approximately {{convert|5|mi|km}} southwest of [[Alice, North Dakota|Alice]].{{Cite web |date=October 6, 2025 |title=The U.S.'s strongest tornado in 12 years hit North Dakota in June, National Weather Service says |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/minnesota/news/first-us-ef5-tornado-12-years-north-dakota/ |access-date=October 7, 2025 |website=[[CBS News]] |language=en-US}} {{Multiple image | direction = horizontal | image1 = Enderlin, North Dakota EF5 tornado.jpg | alt1 = A dark photograph of a large tornado illuminated by a distant lightning flash | image2 = Enderlin EF5 Tornado crossing ND 46.png | total_width = 400 | footer = The tornado, seen southeast of Enderlin | alt2 = A grainy VHS still of a large wedge tornado illuminated by a lightning flash. A wall cloud is visible. | align = left }} Overall, the tornado was on the ground for 19 minutes, had a path length of {{Convert|12.10|mi|km|abbr=out}}, and reached a peak width of {{Convert|1.05|mi|km|abbr=out}}.{{Cite web |last=Raza |first=Sarah |date=October 6, 2025 |title=EF5 tornado that killed 3 in North Dakota was the nation's first in 12 years |url=https://www.expressnews.com/news/article/a-tornado-in-north-dakota-was-first-with-ef5-21086828.php |access-date=October 7, 2025 |website=[[San Antonio Express-News]]}} According to the Enderlin–Sheldon Fire Department, 10 homes sustained some form of damage from the storm.{{Cite web |last=Froslie |first=Erin Hemme |date=June 25, 2025 |title=Governor pledges state support for storm victims while touring eastern North Dakota damage |url=https://northdakotamonitor.com/2025/06/25/governor-pledges-state-support-for-storm-victims-while-touring-eastern-north-dakota-damage/ |access-date=October 7, 2025 |website=[[North Dakota Monitor]] |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |last=Schneider |first=Clare Marie |date=June 21, 2025 |title=At least three people dead from a tornado in North Dakota |url=https://www.nhpr.org/2025-06-21/at-least-three-people-dead-from-a-tornado-in-north-dakota |access-date=October 8, 2025 |website=[[New Hampshire Public Radio]] |language=en}} Shortly after the dissipation of the Enderlin tornado, a second large tornado formed just east of the first tornado's path at 11:22 p.m. CDT. Moving southeast, this second tornado caused EF2 damage to trees and outbuildings across a {{Convert|6.82|mi|km}} path before dissipating at 11:34 p.m. CDT. {{clear}} ==Aftermath== === Casualties and recovery efforts === [[File:EnderlinTreeDamage.png|alt=An uprooted trees in a small field of grass; the roots are facing the camera.|thumb|EF4-rated [[root ball]] displacement caused by the tornado.]] Governor of North Dakota [[Kelly Armstrong]] declared a statewide disaster following the tornado, activating the state's "Emergency Operations Plan". The National Weather Service office in [[Grand Forks]], North Dakota, originally gave the tornado an EF3 rating.{{cite news |last1=Cappucci |first1=Matthew |author1-link=Matthew Cappucci |title=A June tornado turned out to be a rare EF5. Why that's surprising — and important |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/weather/2025/10/11/north-dakota-tornado-ef5-rare-rating/ |access-date=October 12, 2025 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=October 11, 2025}} Peak winds were estimated to be around {{Convert|160|mph|kph}}.{{Cite web |last=Nelson |first=T. J. |date=June 24, 2025 |title=Enderlin saw two tornadoes hit on Friday night, the first one was the strongest at a preliminary F3 |url=https://www.kvrr.com/2025/06/23/enderlin-saw-two-tornadoes-hit-on-friday-night-the-first-one-was-the-strongest-at-a-preliminary-f3/ |access-date=October 7, 2025 |website=[[KVRR]] |language=en-US}}[[File: Violent EF5 damage to several full grain train cars near Enderlin.png|thumb|EF5-rated damage to several full grain train cars and empty tank cars tossed and derailed near Enderlin.|alt=An aerial photograph of a field, with a tipped-over train car being visible.]] On October 6, 2025, the [[National Weather Service Grand Forks, North Dakota|NWS Grand Forks]], with assistance from several engineers including [[Timothy P. Marshall]],{{Cite web |last=Sanders |first=Brendan |date=October 7, 2025 |title=First EF5 tornado in 12 years confirmed in North Dakota, here's a history |url=https://www.lmtonline.com/news/article/enderlin-nd-ef5-tornado-history-21088531.php |access-date=October 9, 2025 |website=[[Laredo Morning Times]]}} released a revised survey of the Enderlin tornado. Its final rating was upgraded to EF5 on the [[Enhanced Fujita scale]], with maximum winds estimated to be over {{convert|210|mph|km/h m/s}}. The tornado also caused high-end damage in other areas, although the construction at these areas limited said damage points to being upgraded from high-end EF3 to mid-range EF4. The strong winds correlated to the indicated winds on the [[WSR-88D]] Storm-Relative Velocity data from the Grand Forks radar site.{{Cite web |title=...Enderlin Tornado #1 Upgraded to EF-5... |url=https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=PNSFGF&e=202510061430 |access-date=October 6, 2025 |website=Iowa Environmental Mesonet |language=en-US}} The intensity of the tornado was calculated from the distances the train cars were lofted and thrown. This new method was outlined in a study authored by a team of scientists and engineers of the [[Northern Tornadoes Project]], and published in the peer-reviewed journal ''[[Monthly Weather Review]]'' in 2024.{{Cite web |date=October 6, 2025 |title=Research assists with rating historic EF5 tornado in northern United States |url=https://news.westernu.ca/2025/10/ef5-tornado-enderlin/ |access-date=October 6, 2025 |website=Western News |language=en-CA}} In this study, researchers with the Northern Tornadoes Project found an empirical relationship between the distance large and compact objects, such as farm equipment and vehicles, were thrown by the tornado, and damage indicators corresponding to ratings on the [[Enhanced Fujita scale]]. The study used tornadoes throughout [[Canada]] as examples, and found that these tornadoes, which occurred near [[Alonsa, Manitoba]] on August 3, 2018, [[Scarth, Manitoba]], on August 7, 2020, and [[Didsbury, Alberta]], on July 1, 2023, were all most likely of EF5 intensity, based on [[Monte Carlo method|Monte Carlo]] simulations on [[Cumulative distribution function|cumulative distribution functions]] showing the likelihood of lofting at each wind speed based on the weight and distance of objects lofted.{{cite journal |last1=Miller |first1=Connell S. |last2=Kopp |first2=Gregory A. |last3=Sills |first3=David M.L. |last4=Butt |first4=Daniel G. |date=August 1, 2024 |title=Estimating wind speeds in tornadoes using debris trajectories of large compact objects |url=https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/mwre/aop/MWR-D-23-0251.1/MWR-D-23-0251.1.xml |journal=[[Monthly Weather Review]] |publisher=[[American Meteorological Society]] |volume=-1 |issue=aop |pages=1859–1881 |bibcode=2024MWRv..152.1859M |doi=10.1175/MWR-D-23-0251.1 |access-date=October 7, 2025|url-access=subscription }} In all, it was determined that 33 cars on the train derailed; 19 of them were fully loaded grain hopper cars weighing up to {{Convert|286,000|lb|kg|abbr=on}} that were all tipped over, with one of them being pulled off the tracks and thrown into an adjacent field. The other 14 cars were empty tanker cars weighing up to {{Convert|72,000|lb|kg|abbr=on}}. Four of the cars were thrown out into the field, including one that was tossed {{convert|600|-|1000|ft|m|abbr=on}}, landing {{convert|475.7|ft|m|abbr=on}} away from the previous tank car it was attached to. Wheel sets from the derailed cars detached at the locations where the cars came off the rails. Collaborating with wind damage experts and the [[Northern Tornadoes Project]], the NWS determined that winds of {{convert|230|mph|kph|abbr=on}} were needed to tip over a fully loaded grain car and winds of over {{convert|266|mph|kph|abbr=on}} to throw a tank car {{convert|475.7|ft|m|abbr=on}}.{{Cite web |date=October 6, 2025 |title=EF-5 tornado drought comes to an end after June North Dakota tornado gets an upgrade |url=https://www.wqad.com/article/weather/severe-weather/ef5-tornado-drought-ends-in-the-us/526-887036cb-4703-4455-bcfc-3be30d8aee6d |access-date=October 7, 2025 |website=[[WQAD]] |language=en-US}} In addition, extreme radar measurements were observed around the time that EF5-rated damage was being inflicted. It was also determined that the train cars were lofted twice as far as the EF5 threshold distance and four times heavier than the heaviest object model in the reanalysis. Prior to the reanalysis, the damage to the train cars had been left unrated since train cars are not standard damage indicators.{{Cite web |last=Grand Forks |first=NWS |date=June 26, 2025 |title=Alright chasers/spotters we have completed preliminary surveys and ratings from what we have documented via all of you and completed all planned surveys. We are so far up to 7 tornadoes in our area from Fridays supercells. Tracks and ratings may still be subject to change #ndwx |url=https://x.com/NWSGrandForks/status/1938364523917844827 |access-date=October 20, 2025 |website=[[Twitter]]}} Melinda Beerends, meteorologist in charge of the National Weather Service office in Grand Forks, stated that "In the last kind of 12 years, there's been several strong tornadoes that have come close, but there haven't been known damage indicators at that time to support the EF5 rating {{Omission}} it's hard sometimes to get tornadoes to hit something."{{Cite web |date=October 6, 2025 |title=North Dakota tornado was the first at EF5 strength in a dozen years |url=https://www.wlns.com/top-stories/north-dakota-tornado-was-the-first-at-ef5-strength-in-a-dozen-years/ |access-date=October 7, 2025 |website=[[WLNS]]}} The upgraded rating ended the [[EF5 drought]] that had begun following the May 2013 [[2013 Moore tornado|Moore, Oklahoma, tornado]].{{Cite web |last=Lagrange |first=Jobie |date=October 6, 2025 |title=NWS upgrades Enderlin Tornado to EF-5, ending U.S. "EF-5 Drought" since Moore 2013 |url=https://www.katc.com/weather/nws-upgrades-enderlin-tornado-to-ef-5-ending-u-s-ef-5-drought-since-moore-2013 |access-date=October 7, 2025 |website=[[KATC (TV)|KATC]] |language=en}} The tornado was additionally the first F5 or EF5-rated tornado to occur in the month of June in the United States since the [[1992 Chandler–Lake Wilson tornado|1992 tornado near Chandler, Minnesota]].{{Cite web |last=Morse |first=Ryan |date=October 7, 2025 |title=North Dakota tornado becomes first EF-5 in US since 2013 |url=https://www.wishtv.com/weather/weather-stories/north-dakota-tornado-becomes-first-ef-5-in-us-since-2013/ |access-date=October 11, 2025 |website=[[WISH-TV]] |language=en-US}}{{Cite web
